scenario: A consultant uploads the same client brand guide and contract into a new chat every week before asking for help with that client.
question: Which feature would best remove this repeated work?
options: Research mode, so Claude searches for the files each time
A Project for the client, with the brand guide and contract as knowledge and the standing rules as instructions
An incognito chat, so the files aren't stored
A longer single chat that is never closed
explanation: B is correct: Projects keep instructions and knowledge files together so every chat in them starts with the same context. A is wrong because Research searches the web and connected sources for questions, not to replace a stable reference set. C is wrong because incognito chats aren't available in Projects and keep nothing. D is wrong because one endless chat grows long and drifts.

scenario: A strategy lead needs a cited overview of how five competitors have changed their pricing in the past year, drawn from many sources.
question: Which Claude feature best fits this task?
options: A plain chat with no web access, answering from training knowledge
An artifact, since the output will be long
Account instructions telling Claude to be thorough
Research, with web search turned on, then check the cited sources
explanation: D is correct: Research runs several searches, follows up on findings and returns a cited report, which suits multi-source, current questions. It needs web search on. A is wrong because training knowledge may be out of date and gives no citations. B is wrong because an artifact is an output format, not a way to gather sources. C is wrong because instructions don't give Claude access to current sources.

scenario: An office manager has four Claude tasks this week and wants to use the lightest feature that fits each one.
question: Which task is the best fit for a plain chat, rather than an artifact or a Project?
options: Building a reusable onboarding checklist the team will update monthly
Rewording one email to sound more polite
Running a three-month client engagement with shared reference documents
Creating an interactive budget calculator to share with colleagues
explanation: B is correct: a one-off, short task suits a plain chat. A is wrong because a reusable, updated document suits an artifact. C is wrong because ongoing work with shared documents suits a Project. D is wrong because an interactive tool to share is an artifact.

scenario: A support team drafts several hundred short, routine replies to common questions every day.
question: Which model family is usually the best fit?
options: Opus for every reply, to maximise quality
Whichever model has the newest version number
Alternate between models at random to compare them
Haiku, the fastest and lowest-cost family, suited to high-volume straightforward tasks
explanation: D is correct: Haiku is built for speed and volume on straightforward tasks. A is wrong because the most capable model wastes speed and usage on simple work. B is wrong because version numbers don't tell you which family fits. C is wrong because random switching isn't a selection strategy.

scenario: A strategy director needs to work through a complex pricing decision with many interacting assumptions and trade-offs, once per quarter.
question: Which model family is the best fit?
options: Opus, the most capable family, suited to complex multi-step reasoning
Haiku, because it's fastest
Haiku with a shorter prompt
Any model, since all families reason equally well
explanation: A is correct: Opus is designed for the hardest reasoning, and an infrequent high-value task justifies the extra time and usage. B is wrong because speed isn't the priority here. C is wrong because a shorter prompt doesn't add reasoning capability. D is wrong because the families differ in capability.

scenario: A new team member asks where Sonnet sits among Claude's model families.
question: Which statement about Sonnet is correct?
options: It is the smallest model, used only for classification
It is the most capable model, reserved for the hardest problems
It balances capability and speed, making it a strong everyday choice for most business writing and analysis
It is a feature for searching the web
explanation: C is correct: Sonnet sits between Haiku and Opus as the balanced everyday choice. A is wrong because that describes Haiku, and Haiku isn't limited to classification. B is wrong because that describes Opus. D is wrong because Sonnet is a model family, not a feature.

scenario: A marketing team will generate descriptions for 2,000 products. They're unsure which model to use.
question: What is the best approach?
options: Use the most capable model for all 2,000, just to be safe
Pick the model at random, since the descriptions are short
Test a sample of products on a faster, lower-cost model and move up only if the quality isn't good enough
Generate all 2,000 on every model and compare them all
explanation: C is correct: start with the lightest model that might work, test on a sample, and step up only where quality falls short. Volume multiplies every choice. A is wrong because it may spend far more time and usage than needed. B is wrong because it isn't a decision method. D is wrong because full runs on every model waste effort a sample would avoid.

scenario: A user turns on extended thinking and the highest effort setting for every task, including quick email replies.
question: What is the main drawback?
options: Routine tasks become slower and use more of the usage limit without a meaningful quality gain
Thinking makes Claude refuse simple tasks
Higher effort disables Projects
There is no drawback; higher settings are always better
explanation: A is correct: higher effort and thinking help on complex problems but add time and usage, so they're wasted on routine work. B is wrong because thinking doesn't cause refusals. C is wrong because effort settings don't affect Projects. D is wrong because the trade-off is real.

scenario: An analyst runs a weekly report on a fast model. Recently the reports have needed complex judgements about conflicting data, and reviewers are finding shallow conclusions.
question: What is the most appropriate change?
options: Keep the fast model and add "think harder" to the end of the prompt
Switch every team task to the most capable model
Stop using Claude for reports altogether
Step up to a more capable model, or raise effort, for this report and check whether conclusions improve
explanation: D is correct: when task requirements change, model selection should follow: step up for the task that now needs deeper reasoning, then check the result. A is wrong because wording doesn't add the capability the task needs. B is wrong because one task's needs don't apply to every task. C is wrong because the problem is fit, not the tool.

scenario: After a three-hour planning chat, Claude starts mixing up decisions made early in the conversation.
question: What is the best next step?
options: Keep going in the same chat and correct each mistake
Ask Claude for a summary of decisions and open items, then start a new chat with that summary
Delete the chat and start from nothing
Switch to the fastest model to speed up the chat
explanation: B is correct: long chats drift and use more of the usage limit. Summarising and restarting keeps what matters and clears the rest. A is wrong because the chat will keep growing and drifting. C is wrong because it throws away the decisions. D is wrong because a different model doesn't fix an overlong context.

scenario: A team discussed the agreed launch date in one chat in their Project. In a new chat in the same Project, Claude doesn't know it.
question: Why, and what is the fix?
options: Projects only remember the first chat; delete the others
It's a bug; report it and wait for a fix
Turn on incognito mode so the chats share context
Chats in a Project don't share each other's conversations; add the launch date to the Project's knowledge or instructions
explanation: D is correct: shared context in a Project comes from its knowledge and instructions, not from other chats. Anything needed repeatedly should be saved there. A is wrong because Projects don't work that way. B is wrong because this is expected behaviour. C is wrong because incognito chats are saved to neither history nor memory, and aren't available in Projects.

scenario: A manager wants to ask Claude a one-off sensitive question about a personal matter and doesn't want it saved to chat history or memory.
question: Which option fits?
options: A Project with the question saved in its knowledge
An incognito chat, which isn't saved to history or memory
A normal chat, then ask Claude to forget it
Account instructions telling Claude never to remember anything
explanation: B is correct: incognito chats aren't saved to chat history or memory. A is wrong because it stores the question for reuse. C is wrong because asking Claude to forget doesn't remove a saved chat. D is wrong because instructions don't control what is saved.
